title: How Tight Is the Grip? Explained Simply | PUC Chemistry Class 11
description:
A loose button comes off with one tug, a stitched one needs a hard pull. Atoms hold their outer electrons the same way: some let go easily, some hold on tight. In this animated lesson for PUC and Class 11 Chemistry (NCERT Chapter 3, Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties) Aarav reads the lab chart and wonders why sodium reacts so fast while neon hardly reacts at all.

You will see ionization enthalpy defined piece by piece (X(g) -> X+(g) + e-, always positive, in kJ/mol), then pull the outer electron off a sodium atom on the molecule bench while an energy bar fills to 496 kJ/mol, and see why the second electron is much harder to remove. The first ionization enthalpies of period 2 build live from Li 520 to Ne 2080 kJ/mol (NCERT Exemplar values), we explain the rise step by step, and the two dips: boron below beryllium (2p is shielded more than 2s) and oxygen below nitrogen (paired 2p electrons repel). A worked example turns hydrogen's ground state energy (-2.18 x 10^-18 J) into about 1313 kJ/mol. Then the exam trap, an original JEE Main pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

This is Episode 32 of our PUC Chemistry series.

Made for PUC (Karnataka), CBSE Class 11, NEET and JEE Main students.
